questions.q: Why does this course avoid building around one fictional company?
options: Because a capstone is meant to produce something that's actually the student's own, built under their own name
Fictional companies are against the catalog's content policy for all courses
Because fictional companies are too hard to write realistically
There is no stated reason in the lesson
questions.explain: The lesson states this is intentional: the student builds the project themselves, under their own name, in their own repository, rather than following a scripted fictional scenario.

questions.q: According to this lesson's framework, if you're targeting an applied AI engineer role working with data teams, which project should you polish deepest?
options: Project 3, the tool-using agent
Project 1, the RAG knowledge assistant
Project 2, the AI data analyst (SQL/APIs)
The framework doesn't distinguish between roles
questions.explain: The lesson's role framework maps a data-facing applied AI engineer role to Project 2, since it leans on safe SQL generation and combining structured data sources.

questions.q: Which three fields does each chunk carry per this lesson, and what reads chunk_id back out?
options: text, author, and date — author is read back by Lesson 5
embedding, score, and rank — score is read back by Lesson 4 itself
text, source, and chunk_id — chunk_id is read back by Lesson 6's evaluation
Only text is kept; source and chunk_id are discarded after chunking
questions.explain: Each chunk carries text, source, and chunk_id; the lesson states that chunk_id (along with source) is read back by Lesson 6's evaluation to check whether retrieval pulled the correct chunk.

questions.q: Which of these is explicitly listed as something the README should let a reviewer learn without running any code?
options: The student's personal contact information
A list of every library version installed globally on the student's machine
The exact dollar cost of every API call made during development
The project's evaluation numbers, before and after tuning
questions.explain: The lesson lists architecture, evaluation numbers (before/after tuning), tradeoffs/out-of-scope items, and how to run it as the four things a reviewer should learn from the README alone.

questions.q: Which Qdrant client method does this lesson use for retrieval, and why?
options: query_points(), because the older search() method is deprecated and being removed
search(), because it is the only method that has ever existed
fetch_nearest(), a method unique to this lesson's example
No client method is needed — Qdrant retrieves automatically
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out that Qdrant's current client uses query_points(), since the older search() method is deprecated and scheduled for removal.

questions.q: What is Project 1, as scoped in this lesson?
options: A production-pattern RAG knowledge assistant over a document set the student chooses
A multi-tenant SaaS product serving many customers' document sets
A fine-tuned custom language model trained from scratch
A frontend-only chat widget with no retrieval or generation
questions.explain: The lesson scopes Project 1 as a production-pattern retrieval-augmented generation assistant over a real document set the student picks themselves — not a multi-tenant product or a fine-tuned model.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say "the answers looked fine when I tried a few questions" is not a real evaluation?
options: Because it's a vibe, not a measurement you can re-run and compare after a change
Because trying questions by hand is against the catalog's policy
Because only Claude is allowed to evaluate RAG assistants
Because it takes too long to try even a few questions
questions.explain: The lesson draws a direct line between a vague impression ("it looked fine") and a real evaluation, which produces a specific, re-runnable number you can compare before and after a change.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three defense-in-depth layers this lesson covers?
options: Parameterized queries
A least-privilege, read-only database role
A statement timeout and hard row limit
Encrypting the entire database at rest
questions.explain: This lesson's three layers are parameterized queries, a least-privilege role, and a statement timeout plus row limit. At-rest encryption is a real practice but isn't one covered in this lesson.

questions.q: What distinct risk does this lesson name that the Lesson 10 query validation does NOT defend against?
options: SQL injection through string concatenation
A user attempting to manipulate Claude's reasoning through the wording of their natural-language question itself
The database running out of disk space
The exchange-rate API being deprecated
questions.explain: Query validation defends the generated SQL text, but a cleverly worded question could still attempt to manipulate the model's reasoning -- a different, not-yet-tested risk this lesson flags as an honest limitation.

questions.q: What does the 'description' field of the run_sql_query tool need to specify, per this lesson's real tool definition?
options: Nothing -- the input_schema alone is sufficient
That the connection is read-only and the tool should never be used for anything but SELECT
The user's name and email address
The exact row count the query will return
questions.explain: The description tells Claude what the tool does and its constraints -- here, that it's read-only and SELECT-only -- which shapes what kind of SQL the model generates.

questions.q: Which lesson in this chapter specifically builds the read-only, parameterized database connection?
options: Lesson 8
Lesson 9
Lesson 11
Lesson 12
questions.explain: Lesson 9, 'Connecting to a Database Safely,' is the foundation every later lesson in this chapter builds on.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what question specifically requires both a SQL aggregate and a live API call?
options: "List all customers in the orders table"
"What's this month's total revenue in euros?" -- a SQL aggregate for the revenue, plus a live rate to convert it
"What is the capital of France?"
"Show me the most recent order"
questions.explain: That example needs a SQL-computed total and a live, up-to-date exchange rate -- neither source alone can answer it, which is exactly why enrichment matters.

questions.q: What does setting is_error: true on a rejected tool_result actually do?
options: It deletes the pending approval record
It marks the result as a failure/denial Claude should react to and incorporate into its next response, rather than treating it as normal data
It automatically retries the tool call
It has no functional effect, it's purely cosmetic
questions.explain: is_error signals to Claude that the tool call didn't succeed as requested, so Claude incorporates the reason into its response instead of treating the content as a normal successful result.

questions.q: What are the two things this lesson says make a good fit when scoping your own Project 3 tool set?
options: The cheapest possible API and the simplest possible UI
At least one tool with a real, hard-to-reverse consequence, and a plausible real reason a human needs to be in the loop
Exactly ten tools and no system prompt
A tool that requires no JSON schema at all
questions.explain: A consequential, hard-to-reverse tool plus a genuine reason for human oversight (cost, risk, irreversibility, compliance) is what makes the approval workflow in Lesson 15 meaningful rather than decorative.

questions.q: In the worked example, why does issue_refund's description require that look_up_order run first?
options: Because the Messages API enforces tool call ordering automatically
So the refund is only issued after the order and its paid amount have been confirmed, rather than guessed
Because look_up_order and issue_refund share the same input_schema
It's not actually required -- the description just mentions it in passing
questions.explain: The description explicitly states the refund should only happen after look_up_order confirms the order and amount, reducing the chance of refunding the wrong order or an incorrect amount.

questions.q: Why does this lesson prefer a specific limitations list (e.g., 'no rate limit on approval requests per conversation') over a vague statement like 'could be more secure'?
options: Vague statements are factually incorrect
Specificity is what separates a project that looks thoughtfully built from one that was finished just well enough to demo
The Messages API requires exact wording for limitations sections
Specific limitations are required to pass the lesson's quiz only
questions.explain: A concrete, named gap shows genuine understanding of the system's edges; a vague hedge doesn't demonstrate anything specific about what was actually considered.

questions.q: Why isn't a type-valid amount_cents value (e.g., a positive integer) guaranteed to be a correct one?
options: Integers can never be validated by a JSON Schema
input_schema only checks shape (that it's an integer); it says nothing about whether that number actually matches the order's real paid total
The Messages API rejects all integer inputs automatically
Type validity and correctness are the same thing in this context
questions.explain: Schema validation confirms the input matches its declared type and required fields -- it has no way to know whether the value is factually correct, which is why a separate truth check is needed.

questions.q: Why does a pending-approval store that works fine as a local Python dict break once the agent is deployed?
options: Python dicts are not supported inside containers
A deployed service restarts, redeploys, and often runs multiple instances, so an in-memory dict loses pending requests that haven't yet been resolved
Dicts cannot hold JSON-shaped data
Deployment automatically converts all variables to strings
questions.explain: In-memory state only survives as long as the process does. A real deployment's restarts and multiple instances mean a pending approval recorded only in memory can vanish before a reviewer ever acts on it.

questions.q: What four parts make up the lesson's framework for answering an AI system design question?
options: Budget, team size, timeline, and marketing plan
Requirements, architecture, tradeoffs, and failure modes
Programming language, framework, IDE, and operating system
Company name, job title, salary, and start date
questions.explain: The lesson's framework moves through requirements, architecture, tradeoffs, and failure modes for almost any AI system design prompt.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn against calling notebook-only work "production" on a resume?
options: Because notebooks cannot run Python code at all
Because a resume should be precise about deployment status, and overstating it is a credibility risk
Because notebook-only projects are always lower quality than deployed ones
Because "production" is a reserved keyword in every AI framework
questions.explain: The lesson lists overclaiming "production" status as one of the common mistakes that weakens an AI engineering resume.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should you do before calling a portfolio project "portfolio-ready"?
options: Delete the README entirely so reviewers focus only on code
Remove all eval numbers in case they are later disproven
Add as many buzzwords as possible to the project description
Test every link in the README, since a dead demo link is worse than no link at all
questions.explain: The lesson lists a dead demo link as a common mistake and explicitly instructs testing every link before considering a project finished.

questions.q: What method does the lesson teach for answering most AI engineering interview questions?
options: Memorize one confident, fixed answer to recite for every version of the question
Name the real tradeoff, state your default, and name the condition that would change it
Avoid giving any specific answer and change the subject
Always answer with the longest possible list of buzzwords
questions.explain: The lesson's core method is naming the tradeoff, giving a default answer, and naming what condition would change that answer -- a stronger signal than a memorized one-liner.

questions.q: When evaluating a real job offer, what does the lesson say to look at beyond the headline base salary number?
options: Nothing else matters besides the base number
Only the company's stock ticker symbol
The whole package: base, equity and its vesting schedule, signing bonus, flexibility, and the timeline to the first compensation review
Only whether the office has free snacks
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly lists the whole compensation package -- base, equity/vesting, signing bonus, flexibility, and review timeline -- as what to evaluate, not just the base number.
